> **How to read this.** The shape sets relativities; the chain sets each line's total. The indication is built peril by peril from weather-normalised emerging experience with Part 1's trends, then loaded for cost above the cap. A motor renewal priced at 500 CU by the shape at the 2024 level becomes 500 × 1.014 × 0.988 × 0.995 = 498.4 CU; a new-business policy with the same shape takes the new-business factor too: × 1.114 = 555.4 CU (the excess factor is inside the off-balance). The last row reads as a loss ratio before expenses: expected buildings losses are 1.20 times the premium charged today.

## Exhibit P2-5. The new-business factor and its credibility

|  | Motor | Buildings | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| New-business claims, 2023 to 2024 | 697 | 77 | 102 |
| New against renewal, actual over model (apparent: fitting rows) | 1.143 | 0.812 | 1.305 |
| Z, claim-count standard √(n ÷ 1,082): factor used (H-NS (a)) | 0.80: 1.114 | 0.27: 0.950 | 0.31: 1.094 |
| Severity CV²; pure-premium standard 1,082 × (1 + CV²) claims | 4.15; 5,575 | 7.20; 8,875 | 2.46; 3,746 |
| Z, pure-premium standard: factor (not used) | 0.35: 1.050 | 0.09: 0.983 | 0.17: 1.050 |

Pooled D² on this shape (motor by peril), out of time / cross-validation, by standard: none 0.1447 / 0.1413; pure premium 0.1444 / 0.1414; count 0.1439 / 0.1415; full 0.1429 / 0.1411. Public board: paired check decided before upload (shape before motor by peril), count 0.15312, none 0.15080, full 0.14646; final shape, count 0.15712 against pure premium 0.15657.

> **How to read this.** The 2025 book is 76% new business against 14% in training, so this factor carries more of the 2025 level than any other judgment. In motor, new business ran 1.143 times what the model expects on the training rows. With 697 new-business claims the claim-count standard gives Z = √(697 ÷ 1,082) = 0.80 and a factor of 1 + 0.80 × (1.143 − 1) = 1.114. The factor weights a ratio of cost, for which the textbook standard is the pure-premium one, 5,575 claims: Z 0.35, factor 1.050. Our validation cannot separate the two: on this shape, in motor, the pure-premium standard wins out of time by +2,944 [165, 5,231] and loses in cross-validation by 1,047 [−4,191, 1,423], and the motor excess comes mostly from one year (1.49 in 2023, 0.85 in 2024). The actuary first chose the pure-premium standard (H-NS (b)), then returned to the count standard after both readings on the 2025 book favoured the larger factor (H-NS (a), decided after a board reading).

## Appendix A. Office premium build-up for the 20 reference policies

Office premium = (risk premium + catastrophe load + fixed expense) ÷ (1 − variable expense − commission − premium tax − profit). Risk premium is annual: the row's expected cost ÷ its exposure. Catastrophe load 12% of the risk premium on buildings and contents; fixed expense 85 CU; variable expense 15%; commission broker 20%, direct 0%; premium tax 8%; profit 8%. > **How to read this.** Take buildings policy B00229821 (broker): expected claims cost 359.0 CU a year, plus 12% for catastrophe reinsurance (43.1), plus 85 CU fixed expense, is 487.1 CU (from the unrounded parts). Divided by 0.49, the share left after 15% variable expense, 20% commission, 8% tax and 8% profit, it gives 994.0 CU against 285.6 CU charged today. Most of the distance is the host's expense table: at the broker divisor a motor policy needs 2.04 times its risk premium plus 173 CU, and a property policy 2.29 times plus 173 CU. The acquired broker book is priced well below the technical premium.

## Appendix B. Gender in motor: fairness exhibit

Gender is allowed in this market's pricing (data page). It enters motor only (P2-S (a)), as one factor fitted on emerging rows on top of Part 1's shape, which carries no gender because Part 1's data has none. No other factor was refitted with gender present, so no other relativity absorbs or offsets it.

|  | Women | Men |
|---|---|---|
| Fitting rows (2023 to 2024) | 23,912 | 23,371 |
| Actual over expected, Part 1 shape without the gender factor | 0.865 | 1.136 |
| Actual over expected, with the gender factor (apparent: fitting rows) | 0.996 | 1.003 |
| 2025 rows | 45,262 | 45,259 |
| 2025 average price per policy year, as filed | 560.7 | 741.7 |
| 2025 average price per policy year, without gender (same motor total) | 646.4 | 656.0 |

Men against women, everything else the same: 1.303 [95%: 1.153, 1.478] (2,000 customer resamples).

| Reference policy | Gender | Price as filed | Same driver, other gender | Without gender |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M00161473 | M | 1,420.2 | 1,089.6 | 1,256.1 |
| M00176777 | M | 1,146.0 | 879.2 | 1,013.5 |
| M00185311 | M | 1,112.3 | 853.4 | 983.8 |
| M00167496 | M | 626.6 | 480.8 | 554.2 |
| M00129413 | F | 480.8 | 626.7 | 554.3 |
| M00118569 | M | 655.3 | 502.7 | 579.6 |
| M00153851 | F | 331.9 | 432.7 | 382.6 |

*Prices are annual risk premiums (expected cost ÷ exposure), CU.*

> **How to read this.** Without the gender factor, the Part 1 shape under-prices men's claims cost (1.136 of expected) and over-prices women's (0.865); the factor closes that gap. Two drivers identical in every rated field pay prices 1.30 to 1, men higher. Reference policy M00161473 (M) is priced at 1,420.2 CU a year; the same driver of the other gender would be priced at 1,089.6, and with gender removed and the motor total held, at 1,256.1. Removing gender would move every motor price by the same two ratios, about −11.6% for men and +15.3% for women.

## Appendix C. Weather responses

Each peril's claim frequency responds to its weather measure's deviation from the address's normal (the same address in different years), fitted on emerging rows. The 2025 price multiplies each row by 1 + Σ (peril's share of the line's cost) × (exp(b × deviation) − 1).

|  | Motor | Buildings | Contents |

| Applied | row | one factor per line | row |

> **How to read this.** A contents policy whose address gets one standard deviation (92 mm) more rain than its normal expects 12.9% more flood claims; flood is 29.3% of contents cost, so that policy's price moves by about 3.8%. Realised 2025 weather is used, which a price set before 2025 would not have; it moves each line by at most 2.8% on average. Buildings takes the line's average factor (1.017) on every row, because its shape is the check file's (H-F (b)); its responses are shown because they set that average.
